title: The Sheet That Told the Truth
part: PART FOUR: THE NIGHT OF THE NORTH WIND

pages.text:
*The Owl Alley Sheet, No. 20. Today's news: the ink did not freeze.*

Hachi reached out and placed his large, rough hand on Shin’s head. He did not shake him. He held him there, steady, while the cold air bit at their faces.

"The fault is mine," Hachi said. His voice was not loud, but it carried across the wet ash. "I asked a child to do a man’s work. I was wrong to let him stand alone in the dark."

By now the neighbors had drifted to the doorway, and more stood behind them in the ash. He turned to them. Umekichi stood with his arms crossed, his white apron stained with soot. Osen stood very straight behind him, her jaw tight.

"And the tofu maker did nothing wrong," Hachi added, looking directly at Umekichi. "The wind started it. Not his brazier."

A murmur rolled through the alley, soft and confused, like dry leaves scraping against a stone wall. Umekichi lifted his face. The redness in his eyes was no longer anger. It was shock. Osen’s shoulders dropped. She let the tension leave her body. A single tear cut a clean line through the dust on her cheek. She did not wipe it away. She just looked at her husband, and then at the broken roof, and finally at Haru, who stood small and solid in the middle of the street.
pages.image: Hachi, a gruff man in a dark navy short coat with a towel over his shoulder, places a hand on the head of Shin, a skinny boy in a soot-grey jacket, while Umekichi and Osen watch from behind, standing in a street filled with wet ash and broken wood.

pages.text:
The shop door slid open, and the cold rushed in, followed by Jiro. He wore his yellow silk kimono, bright and clean in the dim light. Under his arm, he held two heavy wooden blocks.

"Use ours," Jiro said, nodding at Father Sota’s carving table. "Ours are faster."

Father Sota looked up. He looked at the blocks, then at Jiro’s serious face. He nodded once.

For the next few hours, the Owl Alley print shop did not sleep. Father carved the correction, his knives clicking softly against the cherry wood. Grandfather Tobei stood at the printing bench, his hand steady on the baren, guiding the pressure. Kichi printed until his arms shook, his moss-green coat damp with sweat. Mother Okiyo mixed the black ink, stirring it until it shone like night sky.

Jiro printed beside them, his yellow sleeve brushing against Kichi’s green one. They did not speak. They did not need to. The paper flew from the block, damp and black, and hung on the lines like a storm of wings. In the doorway, Master Kuroda stood for a long moment with his arms folded, reading the first wet sheet. Then, without a word, he stepped out of his geta and came in.
pages.image: Inside a print shop at night, Father Sota carves a block while Jiro, in a bright yellow silk kimono, prints beside Kichi in a moss-green coat, with Grandfather Tobei guiding the baren and Mother Okiyo mixing ink, blank paper sheets hanging overhead.

pages.text:
At dawn, Bunta and Gohei were already in the street. Bunta’s voice boomed over the frozen ground, ringing off the wooden walls.

"Read it! The truth of the fire!"

He held up the sheet. It did not shout. It did not blame. It listed what began the fire, what stopped it, who lost a shop, and who needed help. It was simple, clean, and true.

Master Ito, the ward headman, stood in the crowd. He wore his dark formal coat, looking stern and neat. He took a copy from Bunta and read it. His eyes moved slowly across the page. He looked at Umekichi, who stood with his head bowed. He looked at Hachi, who nodded once.

"This is fair," Master Ito said. His voice was quiet, but the street went silent. "From now on, I will read the Owl Alley Sheet first. That is the price of being allowed to print."

Haru understood. It was not a gift. It was a promise.
pages.image: In a snowy street at dawn, Bunta, a large man in an indigo-and-white striped kimono and a deep straw hat, holds up a sheet of paper while Master Ito, an elderly man with a small grey topknot in a plain dark navy kimono with a wide obi and a short dark jacket, reads it seriously, with Umekichi in a white work shirt and apron and Hachi in a dark navy short coat beside them, Haru small in front.

pages.text:
The weeks that followed smelled of fresh wood and sawdust. The neighbors raised a new tofu shop, board by board. Captain Daigoro, square and cheerful in his leather-hooded coat, lifted the biggest beam with a grunt that sounded more like a song.

Hachi mended the chimney cap. He hired two new boys to help Shin. Shin worked half a day, then went to school in the afternoons. He was thinner, but he smiled more.

Across the alley, Jiro and Haru began to trade sheets. His were wonderful now. They were true stories that sounded like wonders. A cat caught in a tree. A neighbor who lost a hat. Small things, written with care.

Haru watched them fly across the gap between the shops, fluttering in the gentle wind. They were not weapons. They were bridges. She tapped her brush against her teeth, thinking about how small a piece of paper could be, and how heavy it could feel when it landed in the right hand.
pages.image: Outside a rebuilt wooden shop, Captain Daigoro, a square man in a leather-hooded coat, lifts a large wooden beam while Hachi and Shin watch, with Haru and Jiro standing across the alley, holding blank paper sheets, on a sunny day.

pages.text:
On the eve of spring, the alley threw beans at the door.

"Demons out!" they shouted. "Good fortune in!"

Haru stood in the shop, her thumb healed, her fingers strong. She held a small block of cherry wood. It was not a calendar. It was not a news sheet. It was an owl, carved with care. She inked it, dampened the paper, and laid it down.

Grandfather Tobei stood beside her, rubbing his shoulder. He looked at the block, then at her.

"The edge is truth," he said, his voice dry and soft. "The hand is kindness. You have both at last."

Haru pressed the baren, hard and even. The ink sank into the fiber. She lifted the paper and hung it on the line. It was a warm morning. The ink in the pot was soft and black. It did not freeze.
pages.image: Haru, an eleven-year-old girl in a rust-orange kimono with a vermilion cord in her topknot, rubs a block with a baren while Grandfather Tobei, a thin old man in a blue-grey kimono, watches beside her, with blank paper sheets hanging on lines in the background.
